title: How to Multiply a Table by Sending People to Start Their Own
excerpt: A table that only grows is a crowd. A table that multiplies is a movement. Here is how to send people out before you feel ready to let them go.
body:
There is a moment in the life of a healthy discipleship table when it has to die a small death. The room has grown full and warm. People love being there. They know each other. And the leader faces a choice that will determine whether this becomes a comfortable club or a multiplying movement: do you keep everyone, or do you send some of them out?

The whole logic of the Great Commission is multiplication. Jesus did not gather a crowd and keep it. He poured into a few, and then he sent them, "As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you" (John 20:21). A table that only adds people is doing arithmetic. A table that sends people to start new tables is doing something closer to the way the kingdom actually spreads.

## Build sending in from the start

The time to plan for multiplication is the first week, not the day the room gets crowded. From the beginning, tell people what this is for. Say it plainly: "We're not just doing this for ourselves. The aim is that some of you will start tables of your own." When sending is the stated expectation from day one, it feels like graduation. When it's sprung on a group two years in, it feels like rejection.

The second-generation church grew because Paul did not hoard. He planted, appointed local leaders, and moved on, trusting the Spirit and the people he'd trained (Acts 14:23). If he had kept every convert close, the gospel would have pooled in one city. Instead it spread. Your table is meant to spread the same way.

## Develop the next leaders on purpose

Multiplication runs on leaders, and leaders are made, not found. So watch your table for the faithful ones, the people who show up, who care for others, who are growing, and start handing them pieces. Let one person lead the Bible discussion this week. Let another lead the prayer. Let someone else host the meal at their house.

This is apprenticeship. The person learns to lead by leading while you are still in the room to catch them. Jesus sent the twelve out two by two (Mark 6:7) while he was still with them, debriefed them when they returned, and let them practice the very thing he would later command them to do everywhere. You do the same: give away responsibility in increasing measure until the person realizes, almost without noticing, that they can already do this.

## Watch for the natural seams

Multiplication often follows the contours of life. A few people from your table all live across town, that's a seam. Two of them work the same shift and could host a table for coworkers, that's a seam. A couple has a circle of neighbors who'd never come to your house but would come to theirs, that's a seam. Look for where a new table could reach people your table never will. The point of sending is not to relieve crowding. It is to reach rooms you can't reach yourself.

## Send the leader with a few, not alone

Don't send a new leader out empty-handed. Send them with two or three from the existing table, a core that already knows the rhythm and can carry it into the new room. This is how the new table starts warm instead of cold, with people who already pray simply and study honestly modeling it for the newcomers. It costs you. The people you send are often the ones you'd most want to keep. That cost is exactly the point. "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies," Jesus said, "it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (John 12:24).

## Bless the sending; don't apologize for it

When the time comes, mark it. Don't let it happen by quiet attrition. Gather the table, name what's happening, lay hands on the ones being sent, and pray over them the way the church at Antioch prayed over Paul and Barnabas before sending them out (Acts 13:3). Make the sending a celebration, not a loss. The emotional tone you set will tell everyone whether multiplication is a sad subtraction or a glad obedience. It is the second. Treat it that way.

## Stay connected without staying in control

After you send people out, resist two opposite errors. Don't abandon the new leaders to sink or swim, check in, encourage, coach, be available when they hit the awkward stretch every new table hits. But don't hover and control either. The new table is theirs now, not a franchise of yours. Paul wrote letters and sent help, but he let his churches be churches. Aim for connection without control. A network of related tables, each owned by its own leader, is far stronger than one big table that depends entirely on you.

## Count differently

Stop measuring success by how many people are in your room on Tuesday. Start measuring it by how many rooms there now are. A table of eight that has sent out three new tables has touched far more lives than a table of thirty that has never reproduced. The crowded table flatters the leader. The multiplying table serves the kingdom. Choose the second, even though the first feels better.

## This week

Look around your table and name one person who could lead. Hand them something this week, the Bible discussion, the prayer time, the hosting. Tell them why: "I think God's going to have you leading your own table before long, and I want to help you get ready." Then start watching for the seam, the room, the circle, the set of people your table will never reach but a new one could.

The goal was never a full room. It was an empty chair at your table, because the person who used to sit in it is now setting a table of their own.
